query: A radiomics-derived imaging signature from CT imaging can predict high-risk patients with neuroblastoma.

hypothesis.title: Radiomics-derived CT imaging signature predicts high‑risk neuroblastoma patients
hypothesis.population: Children and adolescents diagnosed with neuroblastoma who undergo contrast‑enhanced CT imaging
hypothesis.intervention: Application of a radiomics-derived imaging signature extracted from CT scans
hypothesis.outcome: Accurate prediction of high‑risk disease status (as defined by established clinical risk criteria)
hypothesis.clinical_context: Risk stratification in pediatric neuroblastoma to guide treatment intensity and prognosis

steps.name: Comprehensive Literature Review & Feasibility Assessment
steps.description: Conduct a systematic review of existing radiomics studies in neuroblastoma and other pediatric cancers. Summarize published imaging signatures, feature extraction pipelines, and machine‑learning methods. Evaluate the availability of contrast‑enhanced CT scans, image quality standards, and prior risk‑stratification criteria (INRG, COG). Perform a feasibility analysis to estimate sample size requirements for training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts.

steps.name: Formulation of Study Objectives & Hypothesis
steps.description: Define the primary objective: to develop and validate a CT‑based radiomics signature that predicts high‑risk neuroblastoma status as defined by INRG/COG criteria. Secondary objectives may include assessing prognostic value for event‑free survival, treatment response, and performing decision‑curve analysis for clinical utility.

steps.name: Study Design & Protocol Development
steps.description: Draft a multicenter, retrospective‑prospective diagnostic accuracy study. Specify inclusion criteria (age ≥18 years, histologically confirmed neuroblastoma, baseline contrast‑enhanced CT within 30 days of diagnosis) and exclusion criteria (poor image quality, prior therapy before CT). Outline the two‑phase design: (1) retrospective training/validation using existing scans from 3‑5 academic pediatric oncology centers, and (2) prospective external validation in a separate cohort. Define endpoints, sample‑size calculations (e.g., target AUC ≥ 0.85 with 95 % CI width ≤ 0.10), and statistical analysis plan.

steps.name: Ethics & Regulatory Approvals
steps.description: Prepare Institutional Review Board (IRB) submissions for each participating site, addressing data privacy, de‑identification, and consent (waiver for retrospective data, informed consent for prospective validation). Register the study on ClinicalTrials.gov and comply with GDPR/HIPAA regulations for international data sharing.

steps.name: Site Selection & Investigator Training
steps.description: Identify 4‑6 pediatric oncology centers with high neuroblastoma case volumes and standardized CT protocols. Conduct investigator webinars covering study objectives, inclusion/exclusion criteria, image acquisition parameters, and radiomics workflow. Provide a detailed imaging manual (slice thickness ≥1.5 mm, arterial phase timing, reconstruction kernel) to ensure harmonized data.

steps.name: Data Acquisition & Image Standardization
steps.description: Collect DICOM CT scans from each site. Apply a standardized preprocessing pipeline: (a) DICOM de‑identification, (b) resampling to isotropic voxel size (1 mm³), (c) intensity normalization using tissue‑based calibration (e.g., aortic lumen), (d) artifact correction (metal, motion). Document scanner models, acquisition parameters, and any deviations in a central registry.

steps.name: Clinical Data Collection & Gold‑Standard Risk Assignment
steps.description: Gather clinical variables required for INRG/COG risk classification: age at diagnosis, stage, MYCN amplification, histopathology, serum ferritin, LDH, and Shimada biology. Assign each patient a ‘high‑risk’ or ‘non‑high‑risk’ label based on the officially accepted criteria. Store data in a secure REDCap database linked to imaging identifiers.

steps.name: Radiomics Feature Extraction Pipeline Development
steps.description: Implement a validated, open‑source pipeline (e.g., PyRadiomics) within a containerized environment (Docker). Steps include: (a) semi‑automatic tumor segmentation on portal‑venous phase CT using a consensus protocol, (b) inter‑observer reproducibility assessment (intraclass correlation coefficient >0.80) on a subset, (c) extraction of first‑order statistics, shape descriptors, texture features (GLCM, GLRLM, NGTDM, GLSZM), and wavelet‑filtered features. Store feature matrices in a centralized repository.

steps.name: Feature Selection & Signature Construction (Training Cohort)
steps.description: Perform dimensionality reduction on the training set (≈60 % of retrospective cohort) using: (a) variance thresholding, (b) correlation analysis (remove one of any pair r > 0.9), (c) univariate association with high‑risk status (Benjamini‑Hochberg adjusted p < 0.05), and (d) recursive feature elimination combined with cross‑validated LASSO logistic regression. Derive a parsimonious radiomics signature (≥10 features) weighted by model coefficients.

steps.name: Model Development & Internal Validation
steps.description: Fit a multivariable logistic regression (or alternative machine‑learning classifier such as Random Forest or Gradient Boosting) using the selected radiomics signature. Apply 5‑fold cross‑validation within the training set to tune hyperparameters and assess discrimination (AUC), calibration (Hosmer‑Lemeshow test, calibration plot), and decision‑curve analysis. Record performance metrics with 95 % confidence intervals.

steps.name: External Validation (Retrospective Cohort)
steps.description: Apply the finalized model to the remaining retrospective cohort (≈40 % of original data) from participating sites that were not used for model training. Compute AUC, sensitivity, specificity, positive/negative predictive values, and calibration slope. Compare model predictions with gold‑standard risk status to evaluate generalizability.

steps.name: Prospective Validation Cohort
steps.description: Enroll newly diagnosed neuroblastoma patients at participating centers over a 24‑month period. Acquire CT scans following the same standardized protocol, extract radiomics features using the pre‑built pipeline, and generate risk predictions in real time (blinded to treating physicians). After definitive risk assignment by standard clinical criteria, assess model performance prospectively, focusing on time‑to‑prediction, feasibility, and impact on clinical decision‑making.

steps.name: Statistical Analysis & Subgroup Exploration
steps.description: Conduct the predefined statistical analysis plan using R or Python. Primary analysis: comparison of AUC between radiomics model and standard clinical risk factors alone (using DeLong’s test). Secondary analyses: (a) incremental value of adding radiomics to clinical model (net reclassification improvement), (b) performance across imaging platforms (different CT manufacturers), (c) effect of tumor location (retroperitoneal vs. cervical), (d) age sub‑groups (<12 months vs. ≥12 months).

steps.name: Health‑Economic & Clinical Impact Assessment
steps.description: Perform a decision‑analytic modeling study to estimate potential cost‑savings if the radiomics signature enables early identification of high‑risk patients and appropriate escalation of therapy. Use quality‑adjusted life‑year (QALY) estimates and incremental cost‑effectiveness ratios (ICERs) based on published pediatric neuroblastoma treatment costs.

steps.name: Data Management, Quality Assurance, and Monitoring
steps.description: Establish a central data coordinating center responsible for data integrity checks, version control of imaging pipelines, and audit trails. Conduct periodic monitoring visits to each site to verify compliance with imaging standards, segmentation reproducibility, and consent documentation.

steps.name: Manuscript Preparation & Dissemination
steps.description: Draft manuscripts describing (a) the development and validation of the radiomics signature, (b) the prospective validation results, and (c) the health‑economic impact analysis. Submit to high‑impact oncology and radiology journals. Present findings at pediatric oncology conferences (e.g., SIOP, ASCO‑Pediatric). Release the radiomics code and de‑identified feature dataset in a public repository (e.g., GitHub, TCIA) to foster reproducibility.

steps.name: Implementation Planning & Clinical Integration
steps.description: If validation is successful, create a clinical decision‑support tool (web‑based or integrated into PACS) that automatically processes CT scans, computes the radiomics risk score, and presents results alongside standard clinical variables. Pilot the tool in one center, gather user feedback, and develop training modules for radiologists and oncologists before broader roll‑out.

result.evaluation:
**Overall Assessment**

The proposed study is a well‑structured, multistage radiomics project that moves from systematic literature review to prospective clinical validation and health‑economic modelling. As a whole it covers the essential elements of a rigorous diagnostic‑accuracy investigation (design, data acquisition, feature engineering, model development, internal/external validation, regulatory compliance, and dissemination). The plan is largely complete, but several items need clarification, risk mitigation, or additional detail before the work can be considered fully feasible and scientifically robust.

---

## Strengths  

| Domain | Comments |
|--------|----------|
| **Scientific Rationale** | The hypothesis (CT‑based radiomics can predict high‑risk neuroblastoma) is clinically relevant; early risk stratification could influence therapy intensity. |
| **Stepwise Design** | Clear progression from literature review → objectives → protocol → retrospective training/validation → prospective external validation, mirroring the TRIPOD‑AI/ML reporting standards. |
| **Multi‑center Approach** | Inclusion of 3‑5 academic pediatric oncology centres for training and a separate centre for prospective validation improves generalisability and addresses spectrum bias. |
| **Standardised Imaging Protocol** | Explicit slice‑thickness, phase‑timing, and reconstruction‑kernel requirements, plus a central preprocessing pipeline, minimise technical heterogeneity – a common pitfall in paediatric radiomics. |
| **Transparent Feature Pipeline** | Use of an open‑source, containerised PyRadiomics workflow, with reproducibility checks (ICC > 0.80) and version control, satisfies FAIR‑data principles. |
| **Robust Model Development** | Combination of variance filtering, correlation pruning, BH‑adjusted univariate screening, and recursive feature elimination with cross‑validated LASSO is appropriate for high‑dimensional data. |
| **Validation Strategy** | Internal 5‑fold CV, retrospective external validation, followed by a true prospective cohort (real‑time blinded predictions) meets the “three‑phase” validation recommended for AI‑based diagnostics. |
| **Statistical Rigor** | Pre‑specified primary endpoint (AUC ≥ 0.85, CI ≤ 0.10) and detailed secondary analyses (net reclassification, subgroup performance, calibration) are in line with FDA‑MAIA and CONSORT‑AI guidance. |
| **Regulatory & Ethics Plan** | IRB waivers for retrospective data, informed consent for prospective enrolment, GDPR/HIPAA compliance, and trial registration are all addressed. |
| **Health‑Economic Component** | Including a decision‑analytic model (QALY, ICER) strengthens the translational impact and is often required for reimbursement discussions. |
| **Dissemination & Reproducibility** | Commitment to open‑source code, de‑identified feature sets, and presentations at major conferences will facilitate external replication. |
| **Implementation Pathway** | Planning a decision‑support tool and pilot‑testing it before rollout demonstrates foresight toward clinical adoption. |

---

## Weaknesses / Gaps  

| Area | Issue | Potential Impact | Recommendation |
|------|-------|-------------------|----------------|
| **Hypothesis Statement** | The `study_goal` field is left blank (“Investigate the hypothesis: ”). | Lack of a concise, testable hypothesis may hinder protocol approval and downstream reporting. | Draft a one‑sentence hypothesis, e.g., “A CT‑based radiomics signature can discriminate high‑risk from non‑high‑risk neuroblastoma at diagnosis with AUC ≥ 0.85.” |
| **Sample‑Size Justification** | Only a target AUC and CI width are mentioned; no explicit numbers of patients per cohort, nor prevalence assumptions. | Under‑ or over‑powered study; may miss required events for reliable model calibration. | Perform a formal power calculation (e.g., using Obuchowski’s method) based on estimated high‑risk prevalence (~30 % in neuroblastoma) and desired precision for AUC. Provide separate numbers for training, internal validation, retrospective external, and prospective cohorts. |
| **Missing Matched Modules** | Several steps (e.g., literature review, ethics, site training, health‑economic analysis) have `matched_module: null`. | May limit automation/traceability if the platform expects module linkage. | Either map these activities to existing modules (e.g., `StudyDesignModule`, `EconomicAnalysisModule`) or create custom wrappers to ensure all steps are tracked in the workflow system. |
| **Segmentation Process** | “Semi‑automatic tumor segmentation” is described, but no specific software, algorithm, or inter‑observer protocol is detailed. | Variability in ROI definition could dominate model performance; reproducibility concerns. | Choose a specific segmentation tool (e.g., 3D Slicer with GrowCut, or a validated deep‑learning model). Define a training set for annotators, conduct a formal ICC analysis on ≥30 cases, and consider a consensus‐mask approach for the final dataset. |
| **Data Harmonisation** | Pre‑processing mentions resampling and intensity normalisation, but no discussion of scanner‑specific bias correction (e.g., ComBat). | Residual batch effects may inflate or deflate performance across sites. | Incorporate a harmonisation step (e.g., ComBat‑Gaussian) after feature extraction, and evaluate its impact on model stability. |
| **Class Imbalance** | High‑risk prevalence is likely <50 %; no plan for handling imbalance (oversampling, cost‑sensitive learning). | Model may be biased toward the majority class, reducing sensitivity. | Apply SMOTE, random undersampling, or use balanced‐loss functions during training; report sensitivity and specificity at clinically relevant thresholds. |
| **Outcome Definition** | The gold‑standard “high‑risk” label relies on INRG/COG criteria, which incorporate several clinical/pathologic factors. Some of these (e.g., MYCN status) may not be known at the time of the baseline CT. | Potential circularity: the model may be predicting a label that already includes imaging‑independent variables, limiting added value. | Clarify whether the model is intended to *replace* or *augment* the existing risk algorithm. Consider a secondary analysis using only variables available at imaging (e.g., stage, age) to isolate the pure imaging contribution. |
| **Prospective Validation Timeline** | A 24‑month enrolment window may be optimistic given neuroblastoma’s relative rarity (≈ 10‑15 new cases per centre per year). | Insufficient sample size for prospectively testing the AUC target. | Conduct a realistic accrual estimate per site; add additional centres or extend the enrolment period if needed. |
| **Regulatory Pathway** | No mention of intended regulatory classification (e.g., FDA SaMD) or pre‑market submission strategy. | Post‑validation implementation may stall without a clear pathway. | Outline early engagement with regulatory bodies (pre‑Submission meeting) and define the software as a Clinical Decision Support (CDS) tool subject to FDA‑2021 guidance. |
| **Statistical Plan Details** | Calibration methods are named, but no plan for recalibration (e.g., Platt scaling) if external validation shows mis‑calibration. | Decision‑curve analysis may be misleading if predicted probabilities are poorly calibrated. | Include a predefined recalibration step using the validation data and report both original and recalibrated performance. |
| **Health‑Economic Model Inputs** | Uses published cost data but does not specify source, perspective (payer vs. societal), or discount rate. | Results may be non‑transparent and not accepted by health‑technology assessment bodies. | Draft a full economic model protocol (Markov or decision tree) with sensitivity analyses on key cost and utility parameters. |
| **Data Governance** | Central data coordinating centre is mentioned, but no concrete data‑sharing agreement (DSA) or use of a Trusted Research Environment (TRE). | Potential legal barriers, especially for international sites. | Establish a DSA and host data in a certified TRE (e.g., UK NHS Safe Haven, US NCI Cancer Imaging Archive) with role‑based access. |
| **Risk Management** | No explicit risk‑mitigation table (e.g., for delayed site start‑up, scanner upgrades, loss of key personnel). | Project timelines could be jeopardised. | Create a simple RAID log (Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies) and assign owners. |
| **Patient/Parent Involvement** | No plan for patient‑focused outcomes, acceptability, or stakeholder engagement. | May affect uptake and funding justification. | Involve a patient advisory panel early to review consent forms, understand concerns about AI use, and co‑design the decision‑support interface. |

---

## Feasibility Verdict  

- **Technical Feasibility:** High. The imaging pipeline uses mature open‑source tools, and the required CT protocol (≤ 1.5 mm slices, arterial/venous phase) is already standard in paediatric oncology centres.  
- **Operational Feasibility:** Moderate. The retrospective component is realistic, but the prospective enrolment may fall short unless additional centres are recruited or the accrual period is extended.  
- **Regulatory Feasibility:** Adequate, provided that site‑specific IRB approvals and data‑transfer agreements are secured early. A pre‑market strategy should be incorporated if the final aim is a clinical‑decision tool.  
- **Statistical Feasibility:** Acceptable if a formal sample‑size calculation confirms ≥ 150‑200 high‑risk cases across all phases; otherwise the AUC CI may be too wide.  

---

## Recommendations for Strengthening the Protocol  

1. **Finalize the hypothesis and primary endpoint** in a single sentence and embed it in the abstract and study registration.  
2. **Perform a detailed sample‑size calculation** based on projected prevalence and desired AUC precision; present numbers for each phase.  
3. **Map all steps to workflow modules** (or create custom modules) to ensure end‑to‑end traceability in the audit system.  
4. **Standardize segmentation** with a defined software, training protocol, and ICC target; consider an automated deep‑learning segmenter to reduce manual workload.  
5. **Add a harmonisation step** (e.g., ComBat) and explicitly address class imbalance in model training.  
6. **Clarify the intended clinical role** of the radiomics signature (stand‑alone vs. additive) and design a secondary analysis that isolates the imaging contribution.  
7. **Re‑evaluate prospective accrual** – add 1–2 more sites or lengthen the enrolment window to guarantee ≥ 100 prospective cases.  
8. **Draft a regulatory pathway** (FDA SaMD, CE‑Mark) and plan a early engagement meeting.  
9. **Expand the health‑economic protocol** with perspective, discounting, and probabilistic sensitivity analysis.  
10. **Implement a robust data‑governance framework** (DSA, TRE) and a risk‑management log.  
11. **Involve patient/parent representatives** to ensure ethical acceptability and to shape the UI of the eventual decision‑support tool.  

---

### Bottom Line  

The study plan is comprehensive, methodologically sound, and aligns well with contemporary standards for AI/ML biomarker development in oncology. Addressing the gaps noted above—especially around hypothesis clarity, sample‑size justification, segmentation reproducibility, class imbalance, and prospective enrolment feasibility—will convert a strong proposal into a fully executable, high‑impact clinical research programme.

query: A radiomics-derived imaging signature from CT imaging can predict high-risk patients with neuroblastoma.

hypothesis.title: CT Radiomics Signature Predicts High‑Risk Neuroblastoma
hypothesis.intervention: Assessment of a radiomics‑derived imaging signature from CT imaging
hypothesis.outcome: Accurate prediction of high‑risk disease status

steps.name: Formulate Research Question and Hypothesis
steps.description: Define the precise hypothesis: A CT‑derived radiomics signature can accurately predict high‑risk neuroblastoma status at diagnosis. Specify primary (e.g., AUC for high‑risk prediction) and secondary (e.g., prediction of event‑free survival) endpoints.

steps.name: Comprehensive Literature Review
steps.description: Search PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and radiomics repositories for prior work on neuroblastoma imaging, radiomics pipelines, and risk stratification. Summarize gaps, methodological standards (e.g., Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative), and benchmark performance metrics.

steps.name: Study Design Selection
steps.description: Choose a multicenter, retrospective‑prospective cohort design. The retrospective arm will provide a training dataset (n≥200), while the prospective arm will serve for internal validation (n≥100) and an external validation cohort (n≥100) from independent institutions.

steps.name: Sample Size and Power Calculation
steps.description: Perform simulations based on anticipated AUC (e.g., 0.85) with α=0.05 and 80 % power to detect a minimum clinically relevant AUC of 0.75. Estimate required number of high‑risk and low‑risk cases (target 1:1 or reflect real‑world prevalence) and inflate for drop‑outs and missing data (~10 %).

steps.name: Ethics, Regulatory Approvals, and Data‑Sharing Agreements
steps.description: Prepare IRB/REC submissions for each participating site, including consent waivers for retrospective data and informed consent forms for prospective enrolment. Draft Data Use Agreements (DUAs) covering de‑identification, GDPR/HIPAA compliance, and secure transfer of imaging and clinical data.

steps.name: Site Selection and Investigator Training
steps.description: Identify 4‑6 pediatric oncology centers with high neuroblastoma volume and standardized CT protocols. Conduct webinars on imaging acquisition standards, DICOM handling, and radiomics workflow (segmentation, feature extraction, quality control). Distribute a detailed operations manual.

steps.name: Eligibility Criteria Definition
steps.description: Inclusion: patients ≥18 years with histologically confirmed neuroblastoma, baseline contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT performed before any systemic therapy, and available MYCN, INSS stage, and serum markers. Exclusion: prior chemotherapy/radiotherapy, CT artifacts precluding segmentation, or incomplete clinical follow‑up.

steps.name: Standardized CT Acquisition Protocol
steps.description: Specify scanner parameters (e.g., 120 kV, 150‑250 mA, slice thickness ≤1.25 mm, portal venous phase 70 s after contrast). Provide phantom‑based calibration guidelines to harmonize voxel size, reconstruction kernel, and noise across sites.

steps.name: Imaging Data Collection and Central Repository Setup
steps.description: Deploy a secure, cloud‑based repository (e.g., REDCap + XNAT) for DICOM upload. Apply automated de‑identification scripts. Record scanner model, acquisition parameters, and timing relative to diagnosis for each case.

steps.name: Tumor Segmentation
steps.description: Perform semi‑automated 3D segmentation of the primary tumor using validated software (e.g., ITK‑Snap, 3D Slicer) with consensus review by two pediatric radiologists. Store masks in NIfTI format. Capture inter‑observer Dice similarity coefficient for a subset (≥30 cases).

steps.name: Radiomics Feature Extraction
steps.description: Extract quantitative features following the Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI) using PyRadiomics. Include first‑order statistics, shape descriptors, texture matrices (GLCM, GLRLM, GLSZM, NGTDM), and wavelet‑filtered features. Apply voxel‑size resampling (1 mm³) and intensity normalization (z‑score) before extraction.

steps.name: Feature Reproducibility and Harmonization
steps.description: Assess intra‑ and inter‑scanner reliability via Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) on a test‑retest subset (n≥30). Use ComBat harmonization to correct for batch effects across centers while preserving biological variance.

steps.name: Clinical Data Integration
steps.description: Collect demographic (age, sex), biologic (MYCN amplification, chromosome 1p/11q status, serum ferritin, LDH), and staging data (INSS, INRG). Encode high‑risk status per current COG criteria (age ≥ 18 months, stage ≥ 4, MYCN amplified, etc.).

steps.name: Dataset Partitioning
steps.description: Randomly split the retrospective cohort into training (70 %) and internal validation (30 %). Reserve the prospective cohort for temporal validation and the external sites for independent validation. Ensure stratification by risk status.

steps.name: Feature Selection and Dimensionality Reduction
steps.description: Apply a multi‑step pipeline: (1) filter out features with ICC < 0.75; (2) remove highly correlated features (Spearman ρ > 0.9) using hierarchical clustering; (3) employ univariate logistic regression (p < 0.05) as a pre‑screen; (4) use penalized regression (Elastic Net) within cross‑validation to select the final predictive set.

steps.name: Model Development
steps.description: Build a predictive model for high‑risk status using logistic regression, random forests, and gradient boosting (XGBoost). Optimize hyperparameters via nested 5‑fold cross‑validation on the training set. Record calibration curves and Brier scores.

steps.name: Model Evaluation
steps.description: Assess discrimination (AUC‑ROC, AUC‑PR), calibration (Hosmer‑Lemeshow test, calibration slope), and clinical usefulness (Decision Curve Analysis) on internal and external validation sets. Compute sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV at clinically relevant thresholds.

steps.name: Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP)
steps.description: Pre‑specify statistical methods, handling of missing data (multiple imputation), adjustment for potential confounders, and subgroup analyses (age < 12 months vs. ≥ 12 months, MYCN status). Include plans for bootstrapped confidence intervals for performance metrics.

steps.name: External Validation and Generalizability Testing
steps.description: Apply the finalized radiomics signature (fixed coefficients) to the external cohort without retraining. Evaluate performance drop‑off and conduct re‑calibration if needed. Perform sensitivity analysis excluding cases with non‑standard CT protocols.

steps.name: Exploratory Prognostic Analyses
steps.description: Correlate the radiomics risk score with event‑free survival and overall survival using Cox proportional hazards models, adjusting for known clinical risk factors. Test for interaction between radiomics score and MYCN status.

steps.name: Clinical Implementation Feasibility Study
steps.description: Prototype a cloud‑based decision support tool that inputs DICOM, runs the automated segmentation‑extraction‑prediction pipeline, and returns a risk probability within 5 minutes. Conduct a pilot usability test with pediatric oncologists and radiologists.

steps.name: Data Management, Quality Assurance, and Monitoring
steps.description: Establish a central data coordinating center. Use REDCap for clinical data, XNAT for imaging, and version‑controlled Git repositories for analysis scripts. Perform periodic audits, monitor protocol adherence, and log any deviations.

steps.name: Manuscript Preparation and Reporting
steps.description: Draft manuscripts following TRIPOD (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis) and CLAIM (Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging) guidelines. Include detailed methods, code availability statements, and supplemental tables for all extracted features.

steps.name: Dissemination and Knowledge Translation
steps.description: Present findings at ISPN, SIOP, and RSNA meetings. Submit the radiomics pipeline as an open‑source package on GitHub with Docker images for reproducibility. Engage with stakeholder groups (parents, clinicians) to develop educational material on the test’s interpretation.

steps.name: Future Directions and Funding Applications
steps.description: Identify gaps (e.g., integration with MRI‑based radiomics, longitudinal monitoring). Prepare grant proposals to expand the model to a multicenter prospective trial evaluating impact on treatment decision‑making and patient outcomes.

hypothesis.population: Patients (typically children) newly diagnosed with neuroblastoma
hypothesis.intervention: Radiomics‑derived imaging signature extracted from diagnostic CT scans
hypothesis.outcome: Accurate prediction of high‑risk disease status (as defined by standard risk‑stratification criteria)
hypothesis.clinical_context: Use of CT imaging biomarkers for early risk stratification and treatment planning in neuroblastoma

steps.name: Define Study Objectives and Hypotheses
steps.description: Articulate primary objective: to determine whether a CT‑based radiomics signature can accurately predict high‑risk neuroblastoma as defined by current INRG risk stratification. Secondary objectives include assessing the added predictive value over standard clinical and imaging factors, and evaluating reproducibility across institutions. Formulate null and alternative hypotheses for statistical testing.

steps.name: Form a Multicenter Consortium and Obtain Ethical Approvals
steps.description: Identify 8‑10 pediatric oncology centers with expertise in neuroblastoma and standardized CT imaging. Establish a steering committee, data‑sharing agreements, and a central Institutional Review Board (IRB) protocol. Submit the study protocol to each site’s ethics committee, ensuring compliance with GDPR, HIPAA, and local regulations for minors.

steps.name: Develop a Detailed Study Protocol
steps.description: Create a comprehensive protocol covering inclusion/exclusion criteria, imaging acquisition parameters, radiomics workflow, outcome definitions, follow‑up schedule, and statistical analysis plan. Include a manual of operations (MOP) that specifies CT scanner models, slice thickness (≥1 mm), reconstruction kernels, contrast timing, and patient positioning to minimize variability.

steps.name: Calculate Sample Size and Power
steps.description: Perform a priori power analysis using anticipated AUC improvement (e.g., from 0.75 to 0.85). Assuming a 30 % prevalence of high‑risk disease, 5 % two‑sided alpha, and 80 % power, estimate that ~300 patients are needed for model development and an independent validation cohort of ~150 patients. Account for 10 % dropout/incomplete imaging, targeting enrollment of 350 and 170 patients respectively.

steps.name: Define Eligibility Criteria
steps.description: Inclusion: children (≥18 years) with newly diagnosed, histologically confirmed neuroblastoma, baseline diagnostic CT performed at a participating site before any systemic therapy, and available INSS/INRG risk classification. Exclusion: prior chemotherapy/radiation, poor‑quality CT (artefacts, non‑standard protocol), concurrent malignancies, or inability to obtain consent.

steps.name: Standardize CT Imaging Acquisition and Data Transfer
steps.description: Distribute a CT acquisition checklist (voltage 120 kVp, tube current auto‑modulated, slice thickness ≥1 mm, intravenous contrast administered per weight‑based protocol). Implement a secure, encrypted DICOM upload portal for de‑identified scans. Perform initial quality control at the central imaging core lab; reject scans not meeting criteria and request repeat imaging if feasible.

steps.name: Radiomics Feature Extraction Pipeline Development
steps.description: Select open‑source software (e.g., PyRadiomics) and define a reproducible pipeline: tumor segmentation (semi‑automatic with manual refinement by two blinded radiologists), preprocessing (resampling to 1 mm isotropic voxels, intensity normalization), extraction of first‑order, shape, texture (GLCM, GLRLM, NGTDM, etc.) and higher‑order wavelet features. Store feature matrices in a central database with version control.

steps.name: Feature Selection and Model Building (Training Cohort)
steps.description: Apply a three‑stage feature reduction: (1) assess intra‑ and inter‑observer reproducibility using ICC (>0.80 retain), (2) remove highly correlated features (Spearman r>0.90) via hierarchical clustering, (3) employ supervised methods (LASSO‑penalized logistic regression, Random Forest) with 5‑fold cross‑validation to identify the optimal subset. Fit a logistic regression model producing a radiomics risk score; calibrate using Platt scaling.

steps.name: Internal Validation and Performance Assessment
steps.description: Use bootstrapping (1,000 replicates) to estimate optimism‑adjusted AUC, calibration slope, and Brier score. Generate decision‑curve analysis to quantify net benefit across threshold probabilities. Compare the radiomics model against a baseline clinical model (age, stage, MYCN status, serum ferritin) using DeLong’s test for AUC differences and net reclassification improvement (NRI).

steps.name: External Validation (Independent Cohort)
steps.description: Apply the finalized radiomics signature without re‑training to the validation cohort (different centers, possibly different scanner brands). Compute discrimination (AUC), calibration plots, and decision‑curve metrics. Conduct subgroup analyses by age (<1 yr vs ≥1 yr), tumor location, and scanner type to assess robustness.

steps.name: Statistical Analysis Plan Finalization
steps.description: Detail all statistical tests, handling of missing data (multiple imputation), significance thresholds, and software (R 4.4+, Python 3.12). Pre‑register the analysis plan on ClinicalTrials.gov and an open repository (e.g., OSF) to ensure transparency.

steps.name: Data Management, Monitoring, and Auditing
steps.description: Implement a REDCap database for clinical variables linked via pseudonymized IDs to imaging files. Appoint a data safety monitoring board (DSMB) to review enrollment, data quality, and adverse events quarterly. Conduct on‑site audits at random to verify adherence to the MOP.

steps.name: Assess Clinical Utility and Implementation Feasibility
steps.description: Engage a multidisciplinary panel (oncologists, radiologists, surgeons, health economists) to evaluate how the radiomics signature could alter treatment pathways (e.g., intensify therapy earlier). Perform a pilot health‑technology assessment estimating cost‑effectiveness and required IT infrastructure for real‑time signature computation.

steps.name: Dissemination of Findings
steps.description: Prepare manuscripts for peer‑reviewed journals (radiology, pediatric oncology, AI in medicine) describing development, validation, and clinical impact. Present at international conferences (ASCO, SIOP, RSNA). Release the anonymized dataset, segmentation masks, and code under a Creative Commons license to foster reproducibility.

steps.name: Plan for Prospective Implementation Trial
steps.description: Based on validation results, draft a protocol for a prospective, randomized controlled trial where treatment decisions are guided by the radiomics risk score versus standard care, to definitively demonstrate outcome benefit (e.g., event‑free survival). Include feasibility milestones and funding strategy.

result.evaluation:
**Overall Assessment**

The proposed mult‑centre radiomics study of neuroblastoma is well‑structured and follows a logical, step‑wise workflow from hypothesis definition to future implementation. The plan demonstrates a solid understanding of the technical, regulatory, and statistical requirements for developing and validating a CT‑based radiomics signature. Below is a concise appraisal of its **strengths**, **weaknesses**, and **key recommendations** to improve completeness, feasibility, and scientific rigor.

---

### Strengths  

| Area | Why it adds value | Comments |
|------|-------------------|----------|
| **Clear objectives & hierarchical hypotheses** | Primary aim (predict high‑risk disease) and secondary aims (added value, reproducibility) are explicitly stated. | Provides a focused analytic framework. |
| **Multicentre consortium (8‑10 sites)** | Increases sample size, heterogeneity of scanners, and external validity. | The steering‑committee and data‑sharing agreement sections are appropriate. |
| **Standardised imaging protocol** | Detailed CT parameters (kVp, slice thickness, contrast timing) minimise acquisition bias. | Linking to the *ImagingProtocolDesigner* module is forward‑looking. |
| **Robust radiomics pipeline** | Uses open‑source PyRadiomics, semi‑automatic segmentation with two blinded readers, ICC‑based reproducibility filter, and hierarchical clustering to reduce redundancy. | Aligns with current best‑practice guidelines (TRIPOD, IBSI). |
| **Statistical design** | Power calculation based on an AUC lift (0.75 → 0.85) with realistic prevalence, bootstrapped internal validation, DeLong test, NRI, DCA, and multiple‑imputation for missing data. | Covers discrimination, calibration, clinical utility, and over‑optimism correction. |
| **Data‑management & QA** | REDCap for clinical data, central imaging core lab, DSMB, on‑site audits, version‑controlled feature database. | Ensures data integrity and regulatory compliance. |
| **Transparency & reproducibility** | Pre‑registration, open‑source code, de‑identified dataset release under CC‑BY‑SA. | Meets FAIR principles and facilitates external replication. |
| **Future‑direction** | Explicit plan for a prospective RCT and health‑technology assessment. | Shows an end‑to‑end translational pathway. |

---

### Weaknesses / Gaps  

| Issue | Potential impact | Suggested remedy |
|-------|------------------|-----------------|
| **Hypothesis statement missing** | The “study_go al” field only says “Investigate the hypothesis: ” – the actual scientific hypothesis (e.g., *H₀: Radiomics signature does not improve AUC beyond clinical model*) is absent. | Draft a concise, testable hypothesis and embed it in the protocol and registration. |
| **Age limit definition** | Inclusion uses “≥18 years” which is a typo for a pediatric cohort; should be “≤18 years” or specify the upper age (e.g., 0‑18 y). | Correct the inclusion criteria. |
| **Sample‑size assumptions** | AUC improvement of 0.10 is optimistic; no justification for the expected effect size (e.g., pilot data, literature). No adjustment for the number of predictor variables (events‑per‑variable). | Conduct a pilot feasibility analysis or cite prior radiomics work; use the EPV rule (≥10 events per predictor) to inform the maximal feature set retained after selection. |
| **Handling of scanner variability** | Although acquisition parameters are standardised, scanner‐specific reconstruction kernels and manufacturers can still affect texture features. | Include a harmonisation step (e.g., ComBat or deep‑learning based domain adaptation) and plan a sensitivity analysis stratified by scanner type. |
| **Segmentation reproducibility** | Two readers are mentioned but not a process for consensus or adjudication of discrepant segmentations. | Add a third expert reader or an arbitration workflow; record inter‑reader ICC for each case. |
| **Missing data plan** | Only “multiple imputation” is noted, but no details on which variables may be missing, the imputation model, or handling of missing CT scans. | Pre‑specify a hierarchical imputation strategy (clinical data first, then imaging features only if scan available) and conduct a complete‑case sensitivity analysis. |
| **Follow‑up definition** | Primary outcome is high‑risk classification at baseline; no longitudinal outcome (e.g., event‑free survival) is defined for the future RCT. | Clarify whether the current study will also capture outcome data (relapse, survival) to enable secondary analyses and to inform the sample‑size for the later trial. |
| **Regulatory & consent specifics** | Pediatric consent/assent procedures are not described; GDPR/HIPAA compliance is mentioned but no concrete data‑transfer security measures (e.g., encrypted VPN, use of a certified cloud). | Outline the consent/assent forms, parental permission, and a detailed data‑transfer SOP with encryption standards (AES‑256, TLS 1.3). |
| **Timeline & resources** | No Gantt‑chart or milestone schedule; feasibility of enrolling 350+ patients across 8‑10 sites in a reasonable time frame is uncertain. | Provide a realistic recruitment timeline (e.g., 24 months enrolment, 6 months QC, 12 months analysis) and a budget summary (person‑hours, imaging core costs). |
| **Health‑economics methodology** | The “pilot health‑technology assessment” is mentioned but lacks methodological detail (cost‑effectiveness model, perspective, willingness‑to‑pay threshold). | Sketch a decision‑analytic model (Markov or partitioned survival) and specify data sources for costs and utilities. |
| **Potential bias from treatment decisions** | Baseline CT could be obtained after a short pre‑operative chemotherapy window in some centers, affecting tumor texture. | Enforce a strict “pre‑treatment” imaging window (≤7 days after diagnosis) and record any neoadjuvant therapy received prior to CT. |

---

### Feasibility Considerations  

| Factor | Assessment | Action |
|--------|------------|--------|
| **Patient pool** | High‑risk neuroblastoma is rare; each centre must contribute ~30‑40 cases to reach 350. | Conduct a preliminary registry audit to confirm enrolment capacity; consider adding 2‑3 additional sites if needed. |
| **Imaging uniformity** | Even with a protocol checklist, older scanners may not achieve ≤1 mm isotropic voxels. | Allow a limited, pre‑defined deviation (e.g., 1‑2 mm) and include slice‑thickness as a covariate in harmonisation. |
| **Segmentation workload** | Semi‑automatic segmentation of 500+ tumors is labor‑intensive. | Explore crowdsourced or AI‑assisted pre‑segmentation with radiologist verification to reduce time. |
| **Data‑sharing logistics** | Secure DICOM upload from multiple countries raises legal hurdles. | Use a vetted, GDPR‑compliant data‑hosting platform (e.g., EDC‑compatible XNAT) with two‑factor authentication. |
| **Funding** | No budget outlined; costs for imaging core, software licences, staff, and DSMB could be substantial. | Identify grant mechanisms (e.g., European Horizon Europe, NIH U01, Cancer Research UK) and incorporate a detailed cost plan. |

---

### Scientific Soundness  

* **Methodology** adheres to the *TRIPOD* and *Radiomics Quality Score* (RQS) recommendations (standardised acquisition, test‑retest reproducibility, external validation, decision‑curve analysis).  
* **Statistical plan** includes appropriate internal validation (bootstrapping) and external validation, which is essential to avoid over‑fitting.  
* **Clinical relevance** is high; a non‑invasive CT signature could supplement molecular risk stratifiers (MYCN, DNA ploidy) and influence early therapeutic intensification.  
* **Potential pitfalls** are the reliance on a single imaging modality (CT) while MRI is also standard in neuroblastoma staging; the lack of integration with existing molecular data could limit incremental value. Consider a combined radiogenomic model as a secondary analysis.

---

### Recommendations (Priority Order)

1. **Finalize the hypothesis statement** and embed it in all registration documents.  
2. **Validate the assumed AUC improvement** with pilot data or meta‑analysis to justify sample size.  
3. **Add a scanner‑harmonisation step** (e.g., ComBat) and plan a stratified analysis by scanner brand.  
4. **Define a concrete consent/assent workflow** and detailed data‑transfer security SOP.  
5. **Develop a realistic timeline and budget**, confirming enrolment capacity at each site.  
6. **Expand the segmentation workflow** to include adjudication and record inter‑observer ICCs.  
7. **Outline the health‑economic model** (perspective, costs, outcomes) for the implementation feasibility study.  
8. **Consider a secondary radiogenomic analysis** that incorporates MYCN status, 11q loss, or serum biomarkers to test additive predictive value.  

---

**Bottom line:** The plan is comprehensive and scientifically robust, but it requires a few critical refinements—particularly around hypothesis articulation, sample‑size justification, scanner variability handling, and operational logistics—to ensure successful execution and credible, translatable results. Implementing the recommendations above will substantially strengthen the study’s feasibility, regulatory compliance, and impact.

query: A radiomics‑derived imaging signature from CT imaging can predict high‑risk patients with neuroblastoma.

hypothesis.title: CT radiomics-derived imaging signature predicts high-risk neuroblastoma patients
hypothesis.population: Patients diagnosed with neuroblastoma undergoing CT imaging
hypothesis.intervention: Application of a radiomics-derived imaging signature derived from CT scans
hypothesis.outcome: Accurate prediction of high-risk disease status
hypothesis.clinical_context: Risk stratification of neuroblastoma using CT-based radiomics analysis

steps.name: Define Study Objectives and Hypothesis
steps.description: Formulate the primary objective: to determine whether a CT‑based radiomics imaging signature can accurately predict high‑risk neuroblastoma status at diagnosis. Secondary objectives may include assessment of the signature’s incremental value over existing clinical and biological risk factors, and exploration of its reproducibility across imaging centers. State the hypothesis explicitly: "A radiomics‑derived imaging signature from diagnostic CT scans predicts high‑risk neuroblastoma with superior accuracy to standard clinical criteria."

steps.name: Assemble Multidisciplinary Study Team
steps.description: Recruit pediatric oncologists, radiologists, medical physicists, data scientists/biostatisticians, pathology experts, imaging technologists, and a clinical trial coordinator. Assign roles for study oversight, imaging protocol standardization, radiomics pipeline development, data management, and regulatory compliance.

steps.name: Obtain Regulatory Approvals and Ethical Clearance
steps.description: Prepare a comprehensive protocol and submit to the Institutional Review Board (IRB)/Ethics Committee at each participating site. Include details on patient consent for use of diagnostic CT images and genetic/clinical data, data privacy safeguards (HIPAA/GDPR), and a justification for any additional imaging if required. Register the study on ClinicalTrials.gov (or appropriate registry) as an observational predictive biomarker study.

steps.name: Develop Standardized CT Imaging Protocol
steps.description:
Create a detailed CT acquisition guideline to be used across all sites, specifying: 
- Scanner models and minimum detector specifications. 
- Patient positioning, breath‑hold instructions (if feasible), and sedation protocols for young children. 
- Tube voltage (e.g., 120 kVp), tube current modulation, slice thickness (≤1 mm), reconstruction algorithm (standard soft tissue kernel), and contrast administration (if part of routine diagnostic work‑up). 
- Quality control procedures (phantom scans weekly) to ensure uniformity. Distribute a protocol manual and conduct training webinars for technologists.

steps.name: Define Study Population and Eligibility Criteria
steps.description:
Inclusion: 
- Patients ≥18 years with histologically confirmed neuroblastoma. 
- Baseline diagnostic CT performed within 30 days prior to any systemic therapy. 
- Availability of complete clinical, laboratory (e.g., MYCN status), and outcome data.
Exclusion: 
- Prior radiotherapy or surgery affecting the primary tumor before the baseline CT. 
- CT images with severe motion artifacts or incomplete coverage of the tumor. 
- Lack of parental/guardian consent.
Document a screening log to track eligibility assessments.

steps.name: Sample Size Estimation
steps.description: Perform power calculations based on anticipated AUC improvement. Assuming an AUC of 0.75 for standard clinical risk models and expecting the radiomics signature to achieve an AUC of 0.85, with α=0.05 and power=0.90, using the DeLong method yields approximately 200 patients (100 high‑risk, 100 low‑risk). Inflate by 10 % to account for dropouts and unusable images, targeting a total enrollment of ~220 patients across 5‑7 tertiary pediatric oncology centers.

steps.name: Patient Enrollment and Informed Consent
steps.description: Implement a centralized enrollment database. Trained study coordinators obtain written informed consent (or assent plus parental consent) before any study‑specific data collection. Record demographic, clinical, laboratory, and imaging schedule details in the electronic case report form (eCRF).

steps.name: CT Image Acquisition and Transfer
steps.description: Acquire diagnostic CT per the standardized protocol. Export DICOM data to a secure, encrypted central repository (e.g., a HIPAA‑compliant cloud platform). Verify receipt, de‑identify images (remove patient identifiers while preserving essential metadata such as acquisition parameters), and log any deviations from the protocol.

steps.name: Tumor Segmentation and Radiomics Feature Extraction
steps.description:
Develop a semi‑automated segmentation workflow: 
- Use validated software (e.g., 3D Slicer, ITK‑Snap) for manual delineation of the primary tumor on axial images. 
- Perform inter‑observer reproducibility testing on a subset (kappa >0.80). 
- Export binary masks and apply a harmonized radiomics pipeline (e.g., PyRadiomics) adhering to the Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI) guidelines. 
- Extract first‑order statistics, shape descriptors, texture features (GLCM, GLRLM, GLSZM, NGTDM, and wavelet‑filtered features). 
- Record feature definitions, version numbers, and extraction parameters in a metadata log.

steps.name: Data Pre‑processing and Harmonization
steps.description:
Apply preprocessing steps: 
- Resample all images to a common voxel spacing (e.g., 1 mm³). 
- Normalize intensity values using z‑score scaling within each patient’s tumor ROI. 
- Conduct ComBat or similar batch‑effect correction across scanners/sites. 
- Perform feature reduction to eliminate low‑variance (<1 %) and highly correlated features (pairwise Pearson r > 0.90) to avoid redundancy.

steps.name: Feature Selection and Model Development
steps.description:
Split the dataset into training (70 %) and internal validation (30 %) sets using stratified random sampling to preserve the high‑risk proportion. Within the training set: 
- Conduct univariate analysis (t‑test or Mann‑Whitney) to pre‑filter features (p < 0.05). 
- Apply regularization methods (LASSO, Elastic Net) with 10‑fold cross‑validation to select the most predictive subset. 
- Build a multivariate predictive model (e.g., logistic regression, random forest, or gradient boosting) incorporating the radiomics signature and optionally clinical covariates. 
- Optimize hyperparameters via grid search and assess model calibration (Hosmer‑Lemeshow test) and discrimination (AUC).

steps.name: Internal Validation and Performance Assessment
steps.description: Evaluate the final model on the held‑out internal validation set. Compute metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, accuracy, and decision‑curve analysis. Compare performance against a reference model using only standard clinical risk factors (age, stage, MYCN amplification, serum ferritin, etc.) by DeLong’s test for AUC differences.

steps.name: External Validation (Independent Cohort)
steps.description: Obtain an independent cohort of neuroblastoma patients from a collaborating institution not involved in model development (minimum 80 patients). Apply the pre‑trained radiomics signature and model without any recalibration. Assess the same performance metrics and report the net reclassification improvement (NRI) over the clinical model. Document any degradation in performance and explore reasons (e.g., scanner differences).

steps.name: Statistical Analysis Plan Finalization
steps.description: Detail all statistical methods in a pre‑registered analysis plan, including handling of missing data (multiple imputation), subgroup analyses (age groups, stage), and sensitivity analyses (alternative segmentation methods, feature extraction software). Ensure a statistician reviews and signs off on the plan before any model fitting.

steps.name: Quality Assurance and Monitoring
steps.description:
Implement routine monitoring: 
- Quarterly audits of imaging protocol adherence and data entry completeness. 
- Inter‑observer reproducibility checks for segmentation performed on 10 % of cases. 
- Continuous review of adverse events related to contrast administration or sedation. 
- Maintain a log of protocol deviations and corrective actions.

steps.name: Data Management and Security
steps.description: Use a validated clinical data management system (CDMS) with role‑based access. Store de‑identified imaging and radiomics data on encrypted servers with regular backups. Ensure compliance with local and international data‑protection regulations. Create a data‑dictionary and a meta‑analysis ready dataset for future collaborations.

steps.name: Interpretation of Findings and Clinical Translation Planning
steps.description: Summarize whether the radiomics signature adds statistically and clinically significant predictive value. Discuss potential integration into existing risk‑stratification algorithms (e.g., International Neuroblastoma Risk Group). Outline steps for prospective validation in a clinical trial and development of a decision‑support tool (e.g., web‑based calculator).

steps.name: Manuscript Preparation and Dissemination
steps.description: Draft manuscripts following STARD‑AI and TRIPOD guidelines for predictive modeling. Target high‑impact oncology or radiology journals. Prepare conference abstracts for ASCO, SIOP, and RSNA. Share the radiomics pipeline code (open‑source on GitHub) and a de‑identified dataset (subject to data‑use agreements) to promote reproducibility.

steps.name: Regulatory and Commercial Exploration (Optional)
steps.description: If performance is robust, engage with regulatory bodies (FDA, EMA) to discuss qualification of the imaging signature as a biomarker. Initiate discussions with industry partners for potential integration into PACS‑based decision support platforms.

steps.name: Study Timeline and Milestones
steps.description:
Create a Gantt chart with key milestones: 
- Protocol finalization & IRB approval (Months 0‑13). 
- Site training & imaging standardization (Months 2‑14). 
- Patient enrollment (Months 4‑24). 
- Image transfer & segmentation (ongoing). 
- Feature extraction & model development (Months 12‑18). 
- Internal validation (Months 18‑20). 
- External validation (Months 20‑24). 
- Data analysis, manuscript drafting (Months 24‑28). 
- Publication & dissemination (Months 28‑30).

result.evaluation:
**Overall Assessment**

The submitted plan is a well‑structured, end‑to‑end roadmap for a multicentre radiomics biomarker study in neuroblastoma. It covers the essential phases (protocol design, regulatory clearance, data acquisition, image processing, modelling, validation, QA, reporting and translational planning) and links many steps to existing audit‑ready modules (ImagingProtocolDesigner, SegmentationModule, ModelingModule, ValidationModule, QAAgent, ReportingAgent).  

Below is a focused appraisal of **completeness**, **feasibility**, and **scientific soundness**, followed by key **strengths** and **weaknesses** that should be addressed before the study is launched.

---

## 1. Completeness

| Domain | Coverage in the protocol | Comments / Gaps |
|--------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| **Study hypothesis & objectives** | Primary and secondary objectives are listed; hypothesis phrased but not fully written (the “Investigate the hypothesis: ” field is blank). | Insert a concise, testable hypothesis statement (e.g., *H₀: The CT‑based radiomics signature does not improve AUC over the clinical model; H₁: It does*). |
| **Regulatory & ethics** | IRB/EC submission, consent, registration on ClinicalTrials.gov. | No mention of Radiation Safety Committee review (important when adding/standardising CT protocols) and of a Data‑Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) for an observational biomarker study. |
| **Study population** | Inclusion/exclusion criteria defined; screening log mentioned. | Age criterion is erroneous (“≥ 18 years”); neuroblastoma is a paediatric disease – should be *≤ 18 years* (or ≤ 21 years depending on site). No clarification on disease stage distribution, or requirement for MYCN status availability. |
| **Sample‑size justification** | Power calculation based on AUC improvement provided (≈ 200). | The calculation assumes equal numbers of high‑ and low‑risk patients; real‐world prevalence (≈ 45‑55 % high‑risk) may affect power. No provision for stratified analysis (age, stage) which would increase required N. |
| **Imaging acquisition** | Detailed CT protocol, scanner specs, QC, training. | Does not address: (i) use of contrast (mandatory vs optional), (ii) pediatric sedation policies, (iii) radiation dose constraints (ALARA), (iv) acquisition of a calibration phantom for each site (required for ComBat harmonisation). |
| **Segmentation & feature extraction** | Semi‑automated workflow, inter‑observer kappa target, IBSI‑compliant extraction with PyRadiomics. | No plan for a central segmentation review or arbitration process; no description of handling multiple lesions or metastatic sites. |
| **Data preprocessing / harmonisation** | Resampling, z‑score, ComBat batch correction, low‑variance & collinearity pruning. | No explicit list of covariates to be used in ComBat (scanner model, site, reconstruction kernel). Also missing a plan for intensity standardisation across contrast‑enhanced vs non‑enhanced scans. |
| **Model development** | Training/validation split, univariate filter, LASSO/Elastic Net, logistic/Random‑Forest/GBM options, hyper‑parameter grid search, calibration checks. | No pre‑specified primary modelling algorithm (choosing after the fact can be perceived as “p‑hacking”). No plan for nested cross‑validation to avoid optimistic bias when feature selection occurs. |
| **Internal & external validation** | Held‑out internal validation; external cohort of ≥ 80 patients, NRI, DeLong test. | External cohort size may be insufficient to reliably estimate AUC with ±0.05 precision; also no strategy for “site‑wise” validation (leave‑one‑site‑out) which is recommended for multisite radiomics. |
| **Statistical analysis plan (SAP)** | Mention of pre‑registration, handling missing data, subgroup & sensitivity analyses. | SAP details are missing (e.g., exact imputation model, criteria for stopping rule if model performance falls below a threshold). |
| **Quality Assurance** | Quarterly imaging audit, reproducibility checks, AE monitoring, deviation log. | No central monitoring plan (remote source‑data verification), no trigger thresholds for re‑training the model if performance drifts. |
| **Data management & security** | CDMS, role‑based access, encrypted storage, data dictionary. | No mention of GDPR “Right to be Forgotten” procedures, nor of a data‑use agreement for the open‑source repository. |
| **Reporting & dissemination** | STARD‑AI, TRIPOD, open‑source code, de‑identified dataset. | No plan for pre‑registration of the analysis code (e.g., OSF) to increase transparency. |
| **Regulatory/Commercial pathway** | Optional FDA/EMA engagement. | No timeline or milestones for biomarker qualification; missing discussion of the “FDA Breakthrough Device” criteria if intended for clinical use. |
| **Timeline** | Gantt‑style milestones (Months 0‑30). | The timeline is optimistic for a multicentre paediatric study; acquisition of 220 patients across 5‑7 sites in 20 months may be unrealistic given disease rarity and consent logistics. |

*Bottom line*: The plan is largely complete but contains several critical omissions (age definition, radiation safety, detailed SAP, external validation strategy, and realistic enrolment timelines) that must be rectified.

---

## 2. Feasibility

| Aspect | Feasibility Rating (1 = low, 5 = high) | Rationale |
|--------|----------------------------------------|-----------|
| **Multicentre coordination** | 3 | Requires harmonised CT protocols, training webinars, and a central imaging repository. Feasible with adequate funding & a dedicated coordinating centre. |
| **Patient recruitment** | 2 | Neuroblastoma incidence ≈ 10 cases/million/year; achieving 220 eligible participants in ≤ 24 months across 5‑7 tertiary centres may be tight, especially with the 30‑day pre‑therapy CT window. |
| **Standardised CT acquisition** | 3 | Technically possible, but paediatric sedation, contrast use, and dose optimisation add complexity. Need robust SOPs and on‑site QA. |
| **Segmentation workflow** | 4 | Semi‑automated tools are mature; inter‑observer reproducibility target (kappa > 0.80) is realistic if a central training set is used. |
| **Radiomics pipeline & computing resources** | 5 | Open‑source libraries (PyRadiomics, scikit‑learn) and cloud compute can handle > 200 cases easily. |
| **Statistical modelling** | 4 | The analytical plan is appropriate; however, the lack of nested cross‑validation could compromise validity. |
| **External validation** | 2‑3 | Securing an independent cohort of ≥ 80 patients, with fully compliant imaging, may be the bottleneck. Early partnership agreements are essential. |
| **Regulatory & data‑privacy compliance** | 4 | Assuming a central IRB or reliance agreements, GDPR/HIPAA safeguards are standard. Needs dedicated data‑protection officer. |
| **Funding & staffing** | 3 | The plan implies a sizeable research team and data‑management infrastructure; realistic budgeting must be confirmed. |

*Overall feasibility*: **moderate (≈ 3/5)** – achievable if the enrollment target is adjusted, age inclusion corrected, and dedicated resources for imaging QA and external data sharing are secured.

---

## 3. Scientific Soundness

1. **Biological plausibility** – CT‑based texture and shape features have been associated with tumour aggressiveness and genomic alterations in other paediatric solid tumours. The hypothesis that a radiomics signature can augment existing risk models (age, stage, MYCN) is reasonable.

2. **Study design** – Prospective, multi‑centre observational design with pre‑specified primary endpoint (AUC improvement) conforms to the STARD‑AI and TRIPOD standards. The internal/external validation split mitigates over‑fitting.

3. **Statistical rigor** – Using DeLong’s test for AUC comparison and NRI for re‑classification are appropriate. However, the current feature‑selection pipeline (univariate filter → LASSO) risks **information leakage** if the filter is applied before the training‑validation split. A nested cross‑validation or use of the training set only for all selection steps is mandatory.

4. **Harmonisation** – The inclusion of ComBat batch correction is a strength, but its performance must be validated (e.g., by visualising distribution of key features pre‑ and post‑ correction). Also, harmonisation should be performed **after** any standardisation of voxel size and intensity scaling to avoid introducing artefacts.

5. **Outcome definition** – “High‑risk neuroblastoma” is defined by the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) criteria, which combine stage, age, MYCN, histology, and biologic markers. The plan should explicitly state that the reference clinical model will be the INRG risk classification, and the radiomics model will aim to predict *the same* high‑risk label at diagnosis.

6. **Potential biases** –  
   * **Selection bias** – requiring a baseline CT within 30 days before therapy may exclude patients who received an MRI‑only work‑up, potentially leading to a non‑representative sample.  
   * **Spectrum bias** – inclusion of only untreated primary tumours; however, many high‑risk patients receive neoadjuvant therapy quickly, reducing eligible numbers.  
   * **Verification bias** – outcome (high‑risk status) is derived from pathology and genetics, not from imaging, thus avoiding verification bias.

7. **Clinical impact** – The plan anticipates a decision‑support tool and integration into INRG. However, a formal health‑economic or decision‑analytic modelling component is missing; without it, the incremental clinical utility may be hard to justify to regulators.

---

## 4. Strengths

1. **Comprehensive, step‑by‑step workflow** covering all phases from protocol to commercialization.  
2. **Use of standards** (IBSI for radiomics, STARD‑AI, TRIPOD) enhancing reproducibility.  
3. **Multidisciplinary team** with clear role allocation; inclusion of a QA agent and reporting agents demonstrates awareness of audit requirements.  
4. **Robust imaging QA** (weekly phantom, inter‑observer kappa, quarterly protocol audits).  
5. **Open‑science commitment** – code on GitHub, de‑identified dataset, pre‑registration.  
6. **Statistical power calculations** based on clinically relevant AUC improvement.  
7. **External validation plan** – essential for generalizability in radiomics.

## 5. Weaknesses / Recommendations

| Issue | Recommendation |
|-------|----------------|
| **Age inclusion typo** | Correct to *≤ 18 years* (or specify exact paediatric age range). |
| **Incomplete hypothesis statement** | Fill the “Investigate the hypothesis:” field with a concise null/alternative hypothesis. |
| **Radiation safety & dose** | Add a Radiation Safety Committee review, specify dose‐reduction strategies (e.g., tube current modulation, low‑dose protocol for younger children), and include cumulative dose tracking. |
| **Contrast use policy** | Explicitly state whether contrast‑enhanced CT is mandatory; if optional, create separate models or stratify analyses. |
| **Sample‑size realism** | Re‑calculate N using the expected prevalence of high‑risk disease and consider extending enrolment to 30‑36 months or adding collaborating international sites to achieve > 250 patients. |
| **Feature‑selection leakage** | Perform all feature‑selection steps **inside** the training fold (nested CV) or use a pre‑defined feature set based on prior literature. |
| **External validation strategy** | Consider *leave‑one‑site‑out* cross‑validation in addition to a single external cohort; target at least 100 external patients to obtain a stable AUC estimate. |
| **Detailed SAP** | Draft a full SAP before data lock: specify imputation model, exact definitions of performance metrics, planned subgroup analyses (age < 12 mo, stage 4, MYCN‑amplified), and criteria for model acceptance (e.g., AUC > 0.80 and ΔAUC ≥ 0.05, p < 0.05). |
| **Timeline realism** | Extend the enrolment window to 30 months; include buffer periods for site onboarding and data‑cleaning. |
| **Regulatory pathway** | Outline a stepwise biomarker qualification plan (FDA’s “Biomarker Qualification Program” or EMA’s “Qualification Advice”) with milestones. |
| **Health‑economic analysis** | Plan a cost‑effectiveness or decision‑analytic model to quantify the value of earlier high‑risk identification (e.g., reduction in unnecessary intensive therapy). |
| **Data‑sharing agreements** | Secure a Data‑Use Agreement (DUA) for the open‑source dataset; include a clear process for data‑access requests and a governance board. |
| **Patient/parent involvement** | Incorporate a patient‑advocacy advisory panel to review consent forms, data‑use policies, and dissemination materials. |

## 6. Bottom‑Line Verdict

The study plan is **well‑conceived and scientifically promising**, showing strong awareness of the methodological rigor required for radiomics biomarker development. With targeted revisions—especially correcting the age inclusion criteria, tightening the statistical workflow to avoid leakage, clarifying imaging safety and contrast policies, and expanding the external validation and enrolment strategy—the protocol will be both **feasible** and **robust** enough to generate high‑quality evidence that could materially influence neuroblastoma risk stratification.
